paragraphs.text: A cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from 2006, made from leaf grown in [Menghai](menghai-county:county-and-factory) County, Yunnan. Raw pu’er is never given the fast fermentation of the ripe style. The leaf was [fried to kill the green](sheng:making) and then dried in the sun. That heat stops most of the leaf’s own enzymes but not all of them, and the activity that survives is what lets the tea keep changing after it is pressed.

At twenty years it has reached the age that many in the trade wait for before they call a raw pu’er [aged](sheng:ageing), though some count from ten. How far any cake has come depends on how it was pressed and [stored](sheng:storage), so the years it has spent in storage are part of its history.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
